newsitem.title: UK: IRA bombing detainee due to give birth this week.
newsitem.headline: IRA bombing detainee due to give birth this week.

text.p: A pregnant IRA bombing suspect held in a British jail awaiting extradition to Germany is due to give birth on Wednesday, an event that could have serious political repercussions.

Roisin McAliskey has been held in Britain's high security Holloway Prison since last year pending extradition to Germany for questioning about an Irish Republican Army mortar attack at a British Army base at Osnabrueck last year.

The 25-year-old prisoner, daughter of former radical Northern Ireland politician Bernadette McAliskey, nee Devlin, has denied any part in the bombing in which buildings were damaged but no one was injured.

But despite a difficult pregnancy and protests from Ireland and Roman Catholic politicians, Britain has refused repeated requests for bail and insisted she remain in prison until her extradition case is heard.
McAliskey was too ill to appear at her latest hearing last week and media reports suggested that she had been confined to a wheelchair and her baby is dangerously small.

"Our view is that McAliskey hasn't been charged with any crime. She was arrested under spurious circumstances and it appears that there is no real evidence against her in Germany," said Machiel Browne, of the POW (Prisoner of War) department of the IRA's Sinn Fein political branch in Belfast.
"She was treated without any regard to her state of health and in a manner that seemed to be reserved for Irish political prisoners," he added.
Browne warned that her case certainly would not help and could harm the fragile Northern Ireland peace process.
"We arrived at the situation where an Irish woman was treated in such a manner so that nobody could have any confidence in (former prime minister) John Major's ability to build peace," he said.
Browne suggested that McAliskey's release with her new baby could amount to a helpful signal from Prime Minister Tony Blair's new government.
"We need a demonstration from the new British government that they are genuine... Her release on bail would be a step in the right direction."
Although still regarded a high-risk prisoner, prison authorities reduced her security categorisation in March, so she will no longer be subject to frequent strip searches.

McAliskey's mother, who was a key figure in the Irish republican movement in the late 1960s and early 1970s and the youngest member of parliament then, has accused Britain of anti-Irish racism in refusing her daughter bail.
Martin McGuinness, the chief negotiator for Sinn Fein, went even further claiming she had been physically and mentally abused during her detention.
"She has been subjected to abuse of a mental and physical nature that is intolerable," McGuinness said after visiting McAliskey last week.

A spokesman for Britain's Prison Service said McAliskey will give birth in an "outside hospital" but would be allowed to keep the infant with her in a special mother and baby unit in the prison like most of the other 100 women who give birth each year while in custody.
Unlike some other maternity prisoners, McAliskey will not be manacled while she is in labour, a practice that sparked outrage in Britain when it was first reported.
Sinn Fein has been barred from Northern Ireland's all-party peace talks, which are due to resume on June 3, until the IRA reinstates a 17-month ceasefire that it broke in February 1996.
